## Preamble

* This presentation is heavily based on [this Confluence
  page](https://ucam-rcs.atlassian.net/wiki/x/AYCfDg) I have written.
* The nitty gritty details on the configurations for the GRTeclyn CI on the CSD3
  A100s can be found in [this Confluence
  page](https://ucam-rcs.atlassian.net/wiki/x/CQCHDg).
* I won't go through how to set everything up step-by-step, but I will give an
  overview of the setup which should be enough information to determine whether
  something similar would be suitable for your projects.
* There are definitely other ways of setting this up, but this is what we do for
  GRTeclyn.

## Why run CI on CSD3?

Free GitHub/GitLab/\<other provider\> CI minutes on ephemeral cloud runners are
great but may not meet the CI needs of your project:

- No [free] **GPU** minutes on GitHub Actions/GitLab CI/CD
- **Performance regression** testing on these cloud runners is unreliable
- Cannot test on **exactly the same** software stack and environment as CSD3

# Code Repository

##

![](./media/diagram_highlight_code_repository.svg)

## UIS GitLab Instance

- UIS has a [GitLab instance](https://gitlab.developers.cam.ac.uk)
  - Good place to host repositories
  - Permissions within RCS are already configured correctly
  - If you leave, someone in the RSE team will still have access to the
    repository and CI configuration
- Adding a self-managed GitLab runner requires **Maintainer** permissions
  - Most RSEs that create projects under the RSE subgroup will only be given
    **Developer** permissions by default
  - You will need to request a permissions upgrade

## External repository mirroring

- GitLab CI/CD for GitHub repositories is a
  [supported use-case](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/ci_cd_for_external_repos/github_integration.html)
- Mirroring other external repositories is also supported.
- :warning: **Security:** anyone with write access to the repository can trigger
  a pipeline which will run on CSD3.
  - Keep write permissions limited to trusted individuals
  - Set codeowners for GitLab CI config files
  - Consider using protected branches to restrict who can trigger pipelines
- :information_source: **Limitation:** pull requests from **fork repositories
  will not trigger a pipeline**
  - This is the main security constraint that enforces the above
  - Ideally there would be a way to approve pipelines from fork PRs, but this is
  [not currently
  supported](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/work_items/5667)

# GitLab CI Infrastructure

##

![](./media/diagram_highlight_gitlab_ci.svg)

## Host server/VM

- The GitLab Runner can be hosted on **any server**
  - If RSE involvement in a project is short-term, consider using the **research
    group's own resources** (or ask them to obtain some)
- If RSE involvement in a project is expected to be long-term, you can consider
  using [Arcus](https://docs.hpc.cam.ac.uk/cloud/userguide/03-nova.html) (RCS
  OpenStack cloud) to host runner VMs
  - Create an instance via the Horizon web interface
  - Create a separate network and router per instance for isolation
  - You may need to open a support ticket to increase resource quotas for the
    RSE project in Arcus
    - Instances, floating IPs, networks, routers
  - You will need to keep this VM up-to-date.

## GitLab Runner

- Install [GitLab Runner](https://docs.gitlab.com/runner/install/index.html) on the host server
- Register the runner: executor type is chosen at registration
  - **SSH executor** — runs jobs directly on CSD3 via SSH; simplest approach
  - **Shell executor** — runs on host, SSHs to CSD3 manually in the script
    - Required if you need to **upload artifacts** to GitLab
- Runner config stored at `/etc/gitlab-runner/config.toml`
  - You can have multiple runners with different configurations on the same host
  - Runners can be tagged and jobs can specify which tags to run on

## GitLab CI workflow

- `.gitlab-ci.yml` — similar concept to GitHub Actions `.github/workflows/`
  - See [documentation](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/ci/)
- :information_source: **SSH executor limitation:** cannot share artifacts between jobs
  - `gitlab-runner` must be present on the remote system to do this
  - Workarounds:
    - Use a **single stage** to build and run the code
    - Store any build artifacts in a shared location on CSD3 (e.g. RDS) and
      retrieve them in later jobs

# CSD3

##

![](./media/diagram_highlight_csd3.svg)

## Service Accounts

- CSD3 service accounts are **exempt from MFA** — required for non-interactive CI use
- Request via a support ticket with:
  - Name, username, purpose
  - SSH public key (generated on the runner host, no passphrase)
  - IP address to connect from (the Arcus floating IP)
  - SLURM accounts and RDS storage (CC the relevant PIs)
- :information_source: Service accounts **cannot launch interactive shells**
  - Must provide a command directly to `ssh`, e.g.:
    ```bash
    ssh<user>@login-icelake.hpc.cam.ac.uk echo "Hello World!"
    ```

## Tips and gotchas

* Similar to when using CSD3 as a normal user, you can build code on the login
  nodes but should run it on the compute nodes by submitting a job to SLURM.
* You can use `--qos=INTR` to request maximum priority (with the usual
  interactive QoS limits). If you have multiple pipelines running concurrently,
  you will need to ensure that they don't submit jobs at the same time
  (e.g. use lock files).
* Use the `-W` flag for `sbatch` to wait for job completion and get the exit
  code.
* NFS mounts (e.g. home directories) are not completely consistent between
  nodes:
  * Write on compute node might not be visible on login node immediately after
    job completion
